sources.title: Kaplan et al. 2020, Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: curl -sSL abs page (HTTP 200, v1 2020-01-23) and arxiv.org/pdf full text via pdftotext
claims: Loss on held-out text follows approximate power laws in non-embedding parameters, dataset size and training compute, in the paper's WebText2 setting
Doubling parameters (data sufficient, trained to convergence) multiplies loss by 2^-0.076 = 0.95
Compute-efficient allocation N ~ C^0.73, D ~ C^0.27: spend most added budget on a larger model
Authors state they have no solid theory for the laws and that trust conditions are unclear (Appendix C); flag that loss gains may not carry to language tasks (Section 8)

sources.title: Hoffmann et al. 2022, Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v1 2022-03-29) and full PDF text
claims: Over 400 models trained; model size and training tokens should scale in equal proportion for compute-optimal training
The paper restates Kaplan's advice as 10x budget -> 5.5x model, 1.8x tokens

Paper's own hypotheses for the difference: fixed training length and learning-rate schedule in Kaplan, smaller models in Kaplan's runs (reported in the article as the Chinchilla paper's explanation, not as settled)
Three estimation approaches are used for the compute-optimal allocation (Section 3, Table 2)
Parametric loss L = E + A/N^a + B/D^b with E read as the entropy of natural text

sources.title: Pearce and Song 2024, Reconciling Kaplan and Chinchilla Scaling Laws (TMLR)
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v3 2024-11-21) and full PDF text
claims: Much (not most) of the Kaplan/Chinchilla discrepancy is attributed to Kaplan counting non-embedding rather than total parameters (vocabulary and position embeddings excluded), combined with analysis at small scale
Optimization scheme (multiple token budgets, cosine decay) affects the coefficients only marginally, counter to Chinchilla's explanation; Hoffmann's suggestion is called incomplete
At larger total parameter counts the embedding share becomes negligible, so the bias is a small-scale effect that inflated Kaplan's parameter exponent

sources.title: Porian et al. 2024, Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models (NeurIPS 2024)
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v4 2025-01-19) and full PDF text
claims: Three factors explain the gap: last-layer (model head) compute cost, warmup too long for small models, scale-dependent optimizer tuning; corrected setup agrees with Chinchilla
Careful learning-rate decay is not essential for the Chinchilla law, contrary to Hoffmann et al.'s hypothesis; the final matching configuration uses a constant learning rate
The head's contribution becomes negligible with scale (Section 5.2); Pearce and Song identify the same last-layer FLOP count issue (Section 5.1)

sources.title: Besiroglu et al. 2024, Chinchilla Scaling: A replication attempt
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v2 2024-05-15) and full PDF text
claims: Using data reconstructed from Chinchilla's plots, the third (parametric) estimate is inconsistent with the first two methods and has implausibly narrow confidence intervals; the re-derivation is compatible with the first two

sources.title: Wei et al. 2022, Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models (TMLR)
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v2 2022-10-26) and full PDF text
claims: Defines emergent ability as present in larger but not smaller models, hence not predictable by extrapolating small models; near-random performance below a scale, above random after
Metrics without partial credit are an incomplete explanation because emergence is also seen on classification tasks
On six BIG-Bench tasks cross-entropy improves where downstream metrics are near random, but this does not explain or predict emergence

sources.title: Schaeffer et al. 2023, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v2 2023-05-22) and full PDF text
claims: Nonlinear or discontinuous metrics create apparent emergence; continuous metrics give smooth predictable change in the cases tested

More than 92% of claimed BIG-Bench emergent abilities in a hand-annotated task-metric-model family list (their reference [32], not the Wei et al. paper itself) appear under Multiple Choice Grade or Exact String Match
Authors state they do not claim large models cannot show emergent abilities; the independence assumption behind the exact-match model is approximate

sources.title: Brown et al. 2024, Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v3 2024-12-30) and full PDF text
claims: Coverage (fraction of problems solved by any sample) grows with sample count over four orders of magnitude, often log-linear
Where answers can be verified automatically (coding, formal proofs), coverage gains translate directly into performance
On MATH with one open-weight model, coverage rises from 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000 while the best of majority vote or reward-model selection only rises from 40.50% to 41.41%

sources.title: Snell et al. 2024, Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v1 2024-08-06) and full PDF text
claims: Difficulty-adaptive allocation of test-time compute improves efficiency over best-of-N by about 2 to 4x on MATH with models fine-tuned for revision and verification (abstract says more than 4x, section 8 says 2 to 4x)

FLOPs-matched comparison with a roughly 14x larger model: test-time compute wins on easy or medium questions or under low inference load, pretraining wins on hard questions or under high inference load (either condition suffices); the two are not 1-to-1 exchangeable

sources.title: Villalobos et al., Will we run out of data? Limits of LLM scaling based on human-generated data
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v2 2024-06-04) and first pages of PDF
claims: Estimates the stock of public human text and forecasts training-data demand: a question about data supply, not about the shape of the loss curve (forecast dates deliberately not reported)

sources.title: Sardana et al. 2024, Beyond Chinchilla-Optimal: Accounting for Inference in Language Model Scaling Laws (ICML 2024)
sources.access: web open 2026-10-03: abs page (HTTP 200, v1 2023-12-31, v3 2025-04-14; comments field and PDF footer: ICML 2024, PMLR 235) and full PDF text
claims: Chinchilla scaling laws neglect the cost of inference
With reasonably large expected inference demand (~1B requests), models should be trained smaller and longer than Chinchilla-optimal (the article does not give the threshold number)

existing_overlap: ai-term-test-time-compute (published) already covers Snell et al. in depth; this article uses Snell and Brown only as the inference-time axis of scaling and links there. ai-term-model-parameters, ai-term-pretraining and ai-term-benchmark are linked, not repeated. No scaling-law article exists in batch 1.
notes: Count uses app.guides.pack_ingest._body_length on the final pack (paragraphs, rich_paragraph text including 24 characters of article-link text, table cells, callout title and text); 2681 without the link text. History: draft 2497, after verify-1 2580, after verify-2 2705. The worked example (5-digit answer, per-digit accuracy 50/70/90/95 percent -> 3/17/59/77 percent exact match) is the author's own arithmetic under an independence approximation, labelled illustrative and not measured; diagram bars are 3.6 px per percent on a shared baseline. Kaplan vs Chinchilla causes come from two layers (Hoffmann's own hypothesis and two 2024 follow-ups) that do not fully agree; the article attributes the learning-rate explanation to the Chinchilla paper and states where the follow-ups overlap. The inference-cost point cites Sardana et al. (ICML 2024), which replaced an unreviewed 2026 preprint used in the draft (see notes.md). No model names, prices, cutoffs, leaderboard scores, or model parameter/training quantities. Does not predict whether scaling will hit a wall. Three further 2025-2026 arXiv preprints surfaced by search (2509.23963, 2603.22339, 2608.07222) were read at abstract level only and not used.
